newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait tax slash step in right direction - bankers.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait tax slash step in right direction - bankers.

text.p: Kuwait's bid to trim taxes on foreign firms is a good start but more needs to be done to attract investors, economists said on Thursday.

"It is a step in the right direction," said Randa Azar, chief economist at Kuwait's largest commercial bank, National Bank of Kuwait (NBK). "This shows that Kuwait sees the importance of introducing reform".
Finance Minister Nasser al-Rodhan told Reuters on Wednesday his ministry had prepared a bill to cut the maximum tax bracket on foreign firms to about 30 percent from a current 55 percent.
"It is an important law. We would like to see it passed in the the near future," he said.
Officials expect parliament to discuss the bill early in 1997. The bill requires the approval of parliament and the Emir Sheikh Jaber al-Ahmad al-Sabah before it becomes a law.
But some economists and diplomats said other reforms were needed to help lure foreign capital into the traditionally state-orchestrated economy.
"Ownership limitation is one of the most important issues to solve," said an economist. "Big investors would see the risk too high when they cannot have a controlling stake."
Current laws restrict foreign ownership to a minority stake of less than 49 percent in local firms.
"Profitability is not everything. Investment opportunities are not particularly great with the state dominating the most attractive sector (oil)," said a diplomat.

Foreign firms with annual profits of $1.25 million and above pay a maximum tax of 55 percent according to a 1960s law that diplomats say discourages foreign investments and deprives the oil-rich state of technology transfers.
Bureaucracy and restrictions on importing foreign workers are other hindrances.
"Some investors had to work for six months on licences they needed for a project," said an executive. "The labour market is also narrow in Kuwait."
Kuwait, which a population of two million, depends largely on foreign workers. Most of its expensive native work force is hired by the state.
No tax is levied on profits by wholly Kuwaiti-owned companies or on Kuwaiti shareholders in joint ventures. Kuwaitis and foreign residents do not pay income tax to the state.
